additions.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 62: Logging
additions.quote: must keep logs for at least the following processing operations in automated processing systems
additions.why: A UK statutory logging duty, though not one written for AI: controllers and processors handling personal data for law enforcement purposes must log collection, alteration, consultation, disclosure, combination and erasure, and hand the logs to the regulator on request. Applies only to Part 3 (law enforcement) processing. Amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (words omitted 19 August 2025; 'Commission' substituted 30 September 2026). Sets no retention period.

additions.title: UK GDPR, Article 5: Principles relating to processing of personal data
additions.quote: every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate
additions.why: The binding UK rule nearest to an input-data check: personal data fed to a system must be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date, and the controller must be able to show it. Covers personal data only, and is about the data, not the system's outputs.

additions.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 12: Record-keeping
additions.publisher: European Commission, AI Act Service Desk
additions.quote: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system.
additions.why: The provider-side rule that makes the deployer's log duty possible: a high-risk system must be built to record events, including those relevant to the deployer's monitoring under Article 26(5). A buyer can therefore ask a supplier where the logs are and who holds them. High-risk systems only. Commission's copy of the consolidated text, stated on the page to be based on the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026, with Digital Omnibus changes marked NEW or AMENDED.

additions.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
additions.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre, with the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and international partners
additions.locator: Section 4 'Secure operation and maintenance': 'Monitor your system's behaviour' and 'Monitor your system's inputs'
additions.quote: you monitor and log inputs to your system (such as inference requests, queries or prompts)
additions.why: The UK cyber authority on what to watch once a system is live: outputs and performance, so that sudden or gradual change is seen, and inputs, logged for audit and investigation. Written mainly for providers of AI systems, and about security; voluntary. The PDF carries Crown copyright 2023 and no fuller date.

additions.title: ETSI TS 104 223 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
additions.locator: Clause 5.4.2, Principle 12 'Monitor the system's behaviour', provisions 5.4.2-1 to 5.4.2-4
additions.quote: System Operators should analyse their logs to ensure that AI models continue to produce desired outputs
additions.why: The UK code of practice quoted in the brief, carried into a published technical specification: organisations that deploy AI ('System Operators') log system and user actions, and should read those logs to catch drift and anomalies. Free to download. A voluntary specification framed around security; sets no retention period.

additions.title: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry: Report, Volume 1 (HC 1119)
additions.publisher: Post Office Horizon IT Inquiry (chair: Sir Wyn Williams)
additions.quote: the Post Office maintained the fiction that its data was always accurate
additions.why: A statutory inquiry's finding on what happens when an organisation treats the output of a bought-in system as beyond question: people in the Post Office knew or should have known the system could err, its data was relied on regardless, and many hundreds were wrongly convicted. Horizon was accounting software, not AI; cited for the deployer's duty to check, not for anything about machine learning. A large file (Volume 1 concerns human impact and redress).

additions.title: R (Ayinde) v London Borough of Haringey; Al-Haroun v Qatar National Bank [2025] EWHC 1383 (Admin)
additions.publisher: High Court (King's Bench Division, Divisional Court); The National Archives, Find Case Law
additions.quote: Freely available generative artificial intelligence tools, trained on a large language model such as ChatGPT are not capable of conducting reliable legal research.
additions.why: A UK court on a tool used outside what it can reliably do, with no check on its output: false citations reached the court, and the judges warned of severe sanction for lawyers who use AI for research without verifying it. Concerns lawyers' professional duties; it sets no general rule for deployers.

additions.title: WILDS: A Benchmark of in-the-Wild Distribution Shifts
additions.publisher: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 139; P. W. Koh and others
additions.quote: On each dataset, we show that standard training yields substantially lower out-of-distribution than in-distribution performance.
additions.why: Peer-reviewed evidence for the brief's claim that a supplier's assurances hold only inside the conditions tested: across ten real-world datasets, accuracy fell when a model met data unlike its training data, such as a different hospital. This is the reason for input-data checks and monitoring. A benchmark study of 2021 models; it measures the effect and does not test deployer controls. Only the abstract page was read.

additions.title: Reviewable Automated Decision-Making: A Framework for Accountable Algorithmic Systems
additions.publisher: arXiv (J. Cobbe, M. S. A. Lee and J. Singh); ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2021
additions.quote: to provide a systematic framework for determining the contextually appropriate record-keeping mechanisms to facilitate meaningful review
additions.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper, read in the authors' repository copy. Argues that record-keeping across the whole decision process, human steps included, is what makes later review and legal challenge possible; explanations of the model alone are not enough. Supports keeping logs and deciding in advance what to log. A framework, not an empirical study. Only the abstract page was read.

additions.title: Understanding accountability in algorithmic supply chains
additions.publisher: arXiv (J. Cobbe, M. Veale and J. Singh); ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency 2023
additions.quote: algorithmic accountability discussions must consider supply chains and the difficult implications they raise for the governance and accountability of algorithmic systems
additions.why: Peer-reviewed conference paper by UK authors, read in the authors' repository copy. Explains why the deployer's position is hard: a system bought as a service is produced by several organisations linked by data flows, so no one of them sees or controls the whole. Bears on feeding lessons back to suppliers. Analytical, not empirical. Only the abstract page was read.

additions.title: Model Artificial Intelligence Governance Framework, Second Edition
additions.publisher: Info-communications Media Development Authority (IMDA) and Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), Singapore
additions.locator: Section 3, 'Operations management': data for model development ('Understanding the lineage of data', 'Ensuring data quality'), p.37-38; paragraph 3.25
additions.quote: Organisations are encouraged to understand and address factors that may affect the quality of data
additions.why: International comparator on input data: know where data came from and how its accuracy is kept, check accuracy and completeness, and take care with third-party data of mixed origin. Voluntary, Singapore, and dated 2020, before generative AI was in general use.

rejected.title: ISO/IEC 42001, ISO/IEC 23894 and ISO/IEC 42005 standard pages
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading on all three iso.org pages (42001, 77304, 42005). Not cited.

rejected.title: Australia, Voluntary AI Safety Standard and Guidance for AI Adoption
rejected.reason: No response to three attempts on three industry.gov.au addresses (connection failed). Would have been a comparator on record-keeping. Not cited.

rejected.title: SS2/21 Outsourcing and third party risk management (PRA, November 2024 update)
rejected.reason: Opened. Already carried by the third-party criterion in Domain 1, and SS1/23 on this list covers vendor models more directly. Not added.

rejected.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1
rejected.reason: Read for the risk appetite criterion; adds little here beyond the AI RMF 1.0 already on this list.

rejected.title: Public Accounts Committee, Use of AI in Government (2025)
rejected.reason: HTTP 403 to automated reading. Not cited.

brief_check: Nothing read contradicts the brief. One point of nuance for 'No UK statute sets these duties for AI as such': section 62 of the Data Protection Act 2018 is a statutory logging duty for automated processing systems used for law enforcement, and UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(d) requires accurate personal data; neither is written for AI, so the sentence stands.
